Trikuta Softworks: The Working Agreement

A Chandigarh product manager has four days to decide how her team will make and unmake commitments — before the busiest quarter of the company's short life begins.

ISB Product Management Case Collection · Delivery & Technology

1. The Deadline

On the morning of Thursday, 8 October 2026, Simran Aujla sat in the fourth-floor office of Trikuta Softworks in Chandigarh's IT Park with two documents open on her laptop. One was a half-finished slide titled "PM–Engineering Working Agreement: v1." The other was an email from Vikram Chhabra, the company's New Jersey-based head of sales, with the subject line "Al Manara go-live – need your sign-off by Monday." Al Manara Retail Group, a Dubai-based multi-brand retailer, was about to become Trikuta's largest customer, and its returns-processing volume would roughly triple starting the week after Diwali. Simran had four working days to bring a working agreement to the Friday leadership review — a document that would decide, in effect, who got to change a sprint's plan, and how, for the rest of the fiscal year. She could not present a document the engineering team would not honour, and she could not present one so rigid that Vikram's next urgent client request would break it within a fortnight.

2. Trikuta Softworks

Trikuta Softworks was founded in 2021 by three IIT Ropar classmates who had watched, from inside a Ludhiana apparel exporter's operations team, how badly reverse logistics was handled by growing D2C brands. The company built ReturnLoop, a SaaS platform that automates return authorisation, refund routing and resale grading for online sellers, and sells primarily to mid-sized D2C brands and marketplace sellers who cannot justify the custom tooling that a Meesho or a Nykaa builds in-house. By late 2026 ReturnLoop processed returns for 340 sellers, carried an annual recurring revenue of roughly ₹19 crore, and competed on price and speed of integration against larger warehouse-software vendors such as Increff and Unicommerce, both of which Trikuta's sales deck referenced openly as "the players we out-service." The company employed 74 people, had raised a $6 million Series A from a Gurugram-based fund, and ran engineering out of Bengaluru and Pune while product, design and customer functions were distributed globally — a structure common among Indian B2B SaaS firms chasing both domestic quick-commerce demand and export revenue from the Gulf and Southeast Asia.

The Al Manara deal, signed in July, was Trikuta's first seven-figure-dirham contract and its first real exposure to the retail calendar of the UAE, where Ramadan, the Dubai Shopping Festival and the runup to year-end sales created return-volume spikes that did not line up neatly with the Diwali-to-New Year peak Trikuta's Indian customers already put the platform through. Simran, who had joined as ReturnLoop's second product manager in 2022 and now owned the delivery workflow end to end, understood that the company's next two quarters would ask engineering to absorb two festive peaks back to back, on two different calendars, for customers who did not hesitate to escalate by phone when a bug slipped through.

3. What Had Happened

The immediate trigger for Simran's document was Sprint 34, which had ended nine days earlier in a way everyone at Trikuta was still discussing. Midway through the sprint, Vikram had promised Al Manara's operations director a bulk-refund-approval feature "within the month," without checking capacity with engineering. Simran had accepted the change into the sprint to protect the relationship, reasoning that it was a small UI addition. It was not: the feature touched the refund state machine that Karanbir Sidhu, Trikuta's engineering lead in Bengaluru, and his team had spent three sprints stabilising. Two engineers worked through the second Saturday of the sprint to ship it; a regression in refund calculation reached production four days later and was caught only because Farah Öztürk, the Singapore-based customer success lead, personally reconciled a client's numbers late on a Friday night. No customer money was lost, but the incident cost the team a weekend, a rollback, and, Karanbir told Simran plainly on a call the following Monday, "some trust I'm not sure how to get back on my own."

Karanbir's complaint was not really about the bug. It was that no one on the team could say, with confidence, what happened when a mid-sprint request landed: who decided, who estimated the cost, and who could say no. Ana Krüger, the Berlin-based product designer, raised a related but separate concern — she had not been consulted on the refund-approval UI at all, and a second, unrelated feature had shipped with a screen she had explicitly flagged as unfinished. Priya Raman, the Toronto-based data scientist who maintained ReturnLoop's fraud-scoring model, pointed out that she had been pulled twice in six weeks into "quick" production debugging that had nothing to do with her roadmap, each time losing a full day of model work. None of these were new complaints exactly; what was new was that they had arrived in the same week, right as the company's two biggest peak seasons converged, and right as Simran needed engineering's full confidence to negotiate with Vikram and Al Manara from a position of strength rather than apology.

4. The People

Simran Aujla — Senior Product Manager, Chandigarh
Owns the ReturnLoop roadmap and the relationship between product and engineering. Wants a document that survives contact with a real client emergency, protects the engineering team's ability to plan, and that she does not have to personally referee every time sales makes a promise.
Karanbir Sidhu — Engineering Lead, Bengaluru
Manages seven engineers split across Bengaluru and Pune. Wants any change to an in-flight sprint to come with an explicit statement of what it costs elsewhere, and wants the right to say no without it becoming a fight about being "not a team player."
Ana Krüger — Product Designer, Berlin
Reviews every customer-facing flow before it ships. Wants to be a required checkpoint before engineering starts building, not an afterthought consulted once something has already gone wrong.
Vikram Chhabra — Head of Sales, New Jersey
Closes and grows Trikuta's largest accounts, including Al Manara. Wants engineering to treat a named client commitment as close to sacred, and is frustrated that "process" seems, to him, to slow down exactly the requests that keep the company's revenue growing.

6. The Options

Simran drafted three distinct paths before the Friday review.

Option A: a formal change-control process. Every mid-sprint request, regardless of source, would require a written change request, a re-estimation by the engineering lead, and sign-off from both Simran and Karanbir before it could displace committed work; requests missing this would automatically wait for the next sprint. This would give engineering the predictability Karanbir wanted and make the true cost of client promises visible to Vikram before he made them. Its cost was speed: Al Manara's operations team, used to WhatsApp-speed responses from smaller vendors, might read a documented change window as Trikuta being slow, and Vikram was likely to escalate around the process at the first real emergency, since nothing in the document obliged him to route requests through it.

Option B: a one-page working agreement with a fast-track lane. The document would state plainly that Simran owned what shipped and why, Karanbir owned how and at what estimate, and Ana had a mandatory design checkpoint before build began. Any mid-sprint request would need its cost stated in the same room as the request, using Exhibit 2's method, before being accepted — but one small "fast-track" slot per sprint, capped at roughly two engineer-days, would be reserved for genuine emergencies, decided jointly by Simran and Karanbir within four working hours. This balanced protection with responsiveness but depended on Simran and Karanbir being disciplined about what counted as an emergency, and on Vikram accepting that "urgent" and "fast-track" were not always the same thing.

Option C: elevate a technical partner into the client conversation. Simran could ask Karanbir to join client calls with Al Manara directly, alongside her, so that engineering heard commitments as they were made rather than after. This built trust and shared context fastest, and it matched what Trikuta's own delivery playbook called out as good practice for its largest accounts. Its cost was Karanbir's calendar: at seven-engineers-strong, pulling its lead into recurring client calls across Gulf and US time zones would eat directly into the technical leadership Trikuta needed from him during the coming peak, and it did nothing, by itself, to fix how requests were recorded or estimated once a call ended.

7. Questions for Discussion

  1. What, precisely, failed in Sprint 34 — was it Vikram's promise, Simran's acceptance of it, or the absence of any shared process for either?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, what does the relationship between mid-sprint changes and weekend hours suggest about where Trikuta's real capacity limit sits?
  3. Whose interests does each of the three options protect best, and whose does each leave exposed, given the people described in Section 4?
  4. If you were Simran, what would you bring to Friday's review, and what would you say to Vikram before Monday's deadline to make it work in practice, not just on paper?

8. A Note for the Learner

The working agreement between a PM and engineering exists to answer one narrow but consequential question: how do decisions, estimates and changes flow once a sprint has begun? Left unanswered, that question gets answered anyway, informally, by whoever is loudest or most urgent in the moment — which is exactly what happened when Vikram's promise reached Karanbir's team with no stated cost and no shared owner. The topic is not about installing more agile ceremony; Trikuta's own leadership had already cautioned against "too much agile mechanics" for a team of seven engineers, and Option A's formal change-control process risks becoming exactly that — a documented process that slows the company down without changing anyone's incentives.

A well-reasoned answer treats the agreement as a small number of durable commitments, not a workflow diagram: who decides what ships, who owns the estimate, and what happens — specifically, with numbers, as in Exhibit 2 — when someone wants to change a plan already in motion. Option B does this with the least new process: it names owners, it forces the cost of urgency into the open before a promise is made rather than after a bug ships, and its fast-track lane gives Vikram a legitimate route for real emergencies instead of an incentive to go around the agreement entirely. It also directly answers Karanbir's complaint, Ana's complaint and Priya's complaint with one document rather than three separate fixes. Option C is not wrong, and Simran should still pull Karanbir into the Al Manara relationship where it matters most; but as the primary decision, it treats a symptom — Karanbir being out of the loop — without fixing the mechanism that put him there. The defensible path for Simran going into Friday's review is Option B, brought to the meeting already informally agreed with Karanbir and Ana, so that what leadership approves on Friday is a working agreement the team has already chosen to keep — not one imposed on it a week before its hardest quarter begins.

The PM–Engineering Working Agreement

Decisions, estimates and changes are three different flows between product management and engineering. Most organisations invest almost all of their attention in the second one. The arithmetic says the first and third determine the outcome.

1Two Mondays in July

On Monday 13 July 2026, Aparna Iyer, group product manager for payments at Ekaaksh Money, was asked for a date. Ekaaksh is a Bengaluru consumer fintech with about 6.8 million monthly active users, built on the UPI rails and regulated, in the parts that matter, by the Reserve Bank of India and by NPCI's operating circulars. The company's leadership wanted "Ekaaksh for Business" — a merchant-collections product built on UPI autopay mandates — live before the festive peak that begins with Navratri in mid-October. The date named in the room was Friday 16 October. Aparna's delivery squad had sliced version one into 96 work items, none larger than three days, and had eight weeks of clean throughput history. She could have answered in ninety seconds. She asked for two days instead, which is the first thing worth noticing about her.

That same Monday, 1,100 kilometres north-west in Pune, Rohan Pillai learned that his company had signed a contract three days earlier committing to a date he had never seen. Indrayan Health Systems sells a hospital information system — registration, billing, pharmacy, laboratory, insurance pre-authorisation, and linkage to the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's health-ID infrastructure — to private hospital groups. Deven Marfatia, Indrayan's chief revenue officer, had closed Indravati Hospitals Group: six hospitals, 1,850 beds across Nagpur and Raipur, ₹6.2 crore over three years, of which ₹2.8 crore of licence and implementation revenue recognised at go-live. The contract said go-live on 1 December 2026, with liquidated damages of 0.5 per cent of contract value per week of delay, capped at 5 per cent. Sneha Kulkarni, Indrayan's principal architect, put the honest implementation estimate at twenty-one weeks at the median and twenty-seven at the eightieth percentile. Twenty-one weeks from 13 July is 7 December. Twenty-seven weeks is 18 January.

Neither situation is an estimation problem, although both will be described as one in the post-mortem. Aparna's problem is that nobody at Ekaaksh has written down what happens to a number after she says it out loud. Rohan's problem is that nobody has written down that saying a date to a customer is a decision, and whose. Both are problems of the working agreement — or rather, of its absence — and the argument of this page is that the agreement's real function is not to make estimates more accurate but to shrink the variance around them, and that the clauses which shrink variance most are the ones nobody writes.

2The idea, its history, and the people who disagree about it

A PM–engineering working agreement is a short, written, jointly authored and openly revisable document in which a named product manager and a named engineering team record: the decision rights — which classes of decision belong to whom, what consultation each requires, and what happens if nobody decides; the estimate protocol — what an estimate is, who may produce one, with what stated uncertainty, and what conversions of that number are permitted outside the team; the change protocol — what counts as a change, how it enters the work, what it displaces and what it costs; and the escalation and revision clause — who breaks ties, whose signature above both parties makes the document binding, and on what trigger it is rewritten.

The intellectual history has three roots that grew separately and are still not fully reconciled. The first is Kent Beck's planning game, set out in Extreme Programming Explained (1999): business decides scope, priority and release dates; development decides estimates, technical consequence and intra-iteration sequencing. Beck's contribution was to treat the boundary as the interesting object. The second root is organisational behaviour. J. Richard Hackman's Leading Teams (2002) found that explicit norm-setting at team launch was among the strongest predictors of team effectiveness, and Amy Edmondson's 1999 work on psychological safety supplied the mechanism: a norm exists only if somebody will state it in front of the person it restrains. The third root is the retrospective tradition — Norm Kerth (2001), Esther Derby and Diana Larsen (2006) — where the phrase "working agreement" acquired its current meaning as a written norm a team keeps breaking and has decided to make visible.

What the idea was invented to solve is a specific and recurrent pathology: an estimate given in good faith to a colleague is transported, without annotation, into a context where it functions as a promise; changes arrive in flight and are absorbed silently; and decisions sit unmade because everyone believes someone else owns them. Each of these is individually survivable. Together they produce the familiar state in which engineers feel lied about, product managers feel lied to, and both are correct.

Serious practitioners do not agree on what to do about it. The disagreement is not cosmetic, and the table below states each position in the form of the specific proposition its adherents would and would not sign.

3Mechanics, worked rather than named

Experts do four things. Three of them are widely described. The fourth — decomposing the variance in a date and attributing each part to a clause — is what actually separates practitioners who improve their teams from practitioners who produce documents.

The decision inventory and the decision clock

The inventory is built from observed decisions, not from role descriptions. The team lists every decision that actually occurred in the past month, and for each names a decider, the parties who must be consulted, whether the decision is reversible, and a window inside which it must be made. The reversibility split is the one Jeff Bezos described in his 1997 shareholder letter as one-way and two-way doors: reversible decisions go to whoever is closest to the work and are made fast; irreversible ones carry consultation and a written rationale. The window is the part teams skip, and it is the part that changes behaviour, because it converts "we're still discussing it" into a measurable failure. At Ekaaksh, median decision latency in the June quarter was six days; twenty-two of the thirty-one decisions Aparna later catalogued had no identified owner at all until somebody grew impatient.

The estimate protocol, and the arithmetic it forces

Aparna's squad does not estimate individual items. It slices them to a uniform maximum of three days and forecasts from throughput, which places it squarely in the probabilistic school. Eight weeks of completed items: 7, 5, 9, 6, 8, 4, 7, 6. The mean is 6.5 items per week and the standard deviation is 1.5. Over w weeks, expected completion is 6.5w with a standard deviation of 1.5√w.

The scope is 96 items. Naively, 96 ÷ 6.5 = 14.8 weeks, which from 13 July lands on about 24 October — tantalisingly close to the 16 October target, close enough that a less careful product manager would promise it and negotiate the eight days later. The protocol requires two corrections before any number leaves the room.

The first correction is scope growth. Across Ekaaksh's last four projects, items discovered during build added a mean of 25 per cent to the initial count, with a range from 12 to 46 per cent. These are not estimation errors; they are work that did not exist at planning time — a second reconciliation path NPCI's autopay specification required, a settlement-file format a partner bank changed, a consent screen the compliance team asked for in week five. Applying the historical factor gives 96 × 1.25 = 120 items.

The second correction is the band. At 120 items, the median duration is 120 ÷ 6.5 = 18.5 weeks. For the eighty-fifth percentile, solve 6.5w − 1.036 × 1.5√w = 120, which gives w ≈ 19.5 weeks. From 13 July, the median lands on 20 November and the eighty-fifth percentile on 27 November. The festive peak will be over. The honest answer to "can we have it by 16 October" is no, and it is not close.

So the second question — the useful one — is what can be delivered by 16 October, which is 13.5 weeks away. Expected completion in 13.5 weeks is 6.5 × 13.5 = 87.8 items, with a standard deviation of 1.5√13.5 = 5.5. The eighty-fifth-percentile delivered count is 87.8 − 1.036 × 5.5 = 82 items. But 82 items delivered corresponds to only 82 ÷ 1.25 = 66 items of originally scoped work, because a quarter of what gets built was never in the original 96. Aparna can commit, at eighty-five per cent confidence, to 66 of her 96 items. At even odds she can commit to 70. That is the number she takes into the room.

The change protocol, and why it moves the date more than the estimate does

Here is the step practitioners leave implicit. Aparna's observed throughput of 6.5 items per week is not the squad's capability; it is its capability after absorbing unplanned work, which her logs put at 22 per cent of capacity. If the change protocol reduced that to 10 per cent — not by refusing urgent work but by routing it through a single daily triage with a swap rule — throughput would rise to 6.5 × (0.90 ÷ 0.78) = 7.5 items per week, with the standard deviation scaling proportionally to about 1.73.

And the scope-growth factor would fall too, for a reason that is not obvious. A material share of "discovered" scope at Ekaaksh was late-arriving requirements from compliance and from the partner-bank team — requirements that existed on 13 July but were not surfaced because no clause obliged anyone to surface them before a slice was committed. A decision-rights clause that names compliance as a mandatory consulted party at slice-commitment time converts those items from discovered scope into planned scope. On Ekaaksh's history, that pulls growth from 25 per cent down to about 12.

The same result can be read as a decomposition of the eventual delivery date, which is the form in which it is most useful to a general manager. Take the clean case — throughput 7.5, growth 12 per cent — as the irreducible work: 96 × 1.12 ÷ 7.5 = 14.3 weeks. Holding throughput at 7.5 but letting scope growth run to 25 per cent costs 1.7 weeks. Dropping throughput to the observed 6.5 costs a further 2.5 weeks. The residual gap between the median and the eighty-fifth percentile — genuine forecasting noise, the only part that better estimating could ever address — is one week.

Second-order effects follow, and experts anticipate them. An interrupt budget creates an incentive to classify planned work as an interrupt in order to escape the queue, so the log must record the requester as well as the item. A strict swap rule makes the product manager the visible author of every cut, which raises her political cost and is the usual reason the rule is quietly abandoned in month three; the counter-mechanic is a swap log reviewed by the manager above both parties, so that the cuts are seen as system output rather than as her preference. A decision clock creates decisions made at the deadline with no information, so the clause should permit an explicit deferral with a named new date, which is a decision. And publishing percentiles invites an executive to read the band as incompetence, so the band should always be presented beside the injection rate, which attributes the width correctly.

4When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

A working agreement is not universally appropriate, and the conditions can be written as claims a practitioner can check in an afternoon.

Claim one: membership is stable over the agreement's term. Signatories who leave take the agreement with them; above roughly a third turnover per quarter, what remains is an artefact nobody negotiated. Ekaaksh passes — the squad has been intact for five months. Indrayan passes for the core team but fails for implementation, where consultants rotate between hospital sites; Rohan's agreement therefore has to cover the roles, not the individuals, and be re-signed at each site launch.

Claim two: there is one accountable product manager and one accountable engineering lead for the scope. Ekaaksh passes. A platform team serving four product managers fails this claim outright and needs a different instrument — an allocation and a queue policy rather than a bilateral agreement.

Claim three: enough of the work is plannable for a swap rule to bite. A team whose intake is dominated by incidents — a site-reliability group, a payments-operations team during a settlement failure — has too little plannable capacity for swap discipline to mean anything, and should use work-in-progress limits and explicit classes of service instead. Indrayan's support organisation fails this claim; its build team passes.

Claim four: the manager above both parties signs. Without that signature the document is a private treaty voided by the first executive escalation, which will arrive within the quarter. Aparna can obtain Revathi Nambiar's signature as chief technology officer. Rohan's equivalent is the chief executive, because the counterparty in his most consequential clause is the chief revenue officer, and no signature below that level binds Deven.

Claim five: decision throughput, not architecture, is the binding constraint. If most of the team's waiting is on other teams rather than on its own decisions, Conway's law beats contract law, and the time is better spent moving a service boundary. A cheap test: sample twenty recently completed items and record, for each, the longest single wait and what it was waiting on. If more than half the waiting is external, write a dependency map before writing an agreement.

There are also situations in which the instrument is actively misleading. When the roadmap is wrong, a working agreement makes a team more efficient at building the wrong thing and buys its authors a quarter of praise before the outcome data arrives. When leadership adopts the agreement as a compliance instrument — adherence reported upward, deviations investigated — the clauses become the subject rather than the medium, and engineers stop surfacing bad news early, which is the single behaviour the agreement existed to protect. And during a genuine crisis the agreement should be suspended explicitly and loudly, with a named resumption review, rather than tacitly ignored; tacit suspension is how agreements die, because nobody ever declares them restored.

5Hard edge cases

Multi-product platforms. Ekansh Retail Systems runs one platform team behind four product lines with four product managers. The bilateral form does not survive: what is needed is a quarterly capacity allocation — Ekansh runs 40/25/20/15 — plus a stated buffer of 15 per cent and, crucially, a rule about who spends the buffer. Ekansh's rule is that the platform engineering lead spends it, not whoever asks first, because first-asker allocation reliably rewards proximity rather than value. The second-order effect is that the four product managers begin to negotiate with each other rather than with engineering, which is the intended outcome and takes about two quarters to become normal.

Two-sided marketplaces. Ekashila Bazaar connects weaving clusters in Bhagalpur and Kanchipuram with urban buyers. It has a supply product manager and a demand product manager sharing one engineering group. The scarce resource is arbitration, and the failure mode is silent: without a clause, priority is set by whoever escalates most persuasively, and nobody experiences this as a decision. Ekashila's agreement names the general manager as tiebreaker, sets a standing Wednesday forum, and — the interesting part — supplies a mechanical default: where the two sides cannot agree, the tie goes to whichever side's headline metric is furthest below plan. The mechanical default matters more than the tiebreaker, because it removes the premium on volume.

Regulated products. Indrayan's agreement carries something Ekaaksh's does not: a no-fly list of decisions that may never be classified as reversible and may never be delegated downward, however close to the work the decider is. Anything that changes clinical logic, anything touching patient consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, and anything affecting the ABDM linkage all escalate by default. The change protocol also needs a validation multiplier: a change that is three days of engineering is eight days once regression evidence, release documentation and the customer's own user-acceptance cycle are counted, and a change protocol that prices changes at engineering cost alone will systematically over-admit them.

Hardware plus software. Induvadan Grid Systems in Vadodara builds smart prepaid meters and the head-end software that reads them for state distribution companies. The asymmetry is that hardware has hard freeze dates that software does not: after a design is submitted for Bureau of Indian Standards certification, a change that would take four days in firmware costs a certification cycle. The agreement therefore has to carry a joint freeze calendar with a last-responsible-moment marked per subsystem, and the change protocol becomes date-dependent rather than size-dependent — the same change is cheap in week three and ruinous in week eleven.

AI-native products. Ekagra Labs in Hyderabad extracts structured fields from bank statements and GST returns for lenders. Its estimates are bimodal in a way that breaks both the contract and the forecasting schools: either the model clears the accuracy bar within a week of work or it does not clear it at all, and no amount of throughput history predicts which. Ekagra's agreement replaces the estimate clause for model work with a spike with a kill date and a pre-agreed bar: before the spike starts, the parties write down the evaluation set (2,000 held-out documents), the bar (field-level accuracy at or above 97.5 per cent, silent-error rate at or below 1.2 per cent) and the date on which the spike stops regardless of progress. The second clause Ekagra needs is a decision right that does not exist in conventional teams: prompt and model changes are product decisions that an engineer can make in ninety seconds, and the agreement has to say which of them require the product manager's consent and which are logged and reviewed weekly.

What happens at the seams. Every one of these agreements works inside a team and dies at the boundary between teams. What mature companies say they do is align in quarterly planning. What they actually do is maintain an informal favour economy among senior engineers, in which cross-team work gets done because two principal engineers trust each other, and which is invisible, unmanaged, effective, and completely unable to scale past the point where those two people know everyone. The honest institutional answer is not a bilateral agreement per pair of teams — that is n-squared and nobody maintains it — but a published interface from the platform side: a request queue with a posted lead time, a deprecation policy with a notice period, and a named on-call for consumers. Teams that try to solve seam problems with relationship agreements end up with a beautiful document per pair and the same waiting time.

6Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Variance is the product, not accuracy

The competent practitioner asks the team for a better estimate. The expert asks for the spread of the last ten deliveries before asking anything about the next one, because the spread is what determines whether any commitment can be made, and because the spread is diagnostic of causes the estimate is silent about. The tell-tale sign in the wild: in a planning meeting, the expert's first question is about history, not about the item. The obvious reading — that a wide spread means the team estimates badly — is wrong more often than it is right; wide spreads are usually caused by interruption, by unplanned scope, or by dependency waits, none of which are estimation.

The binding clause is always the one that costs the more powerful party

Any agreement contains clauses that constrain engineering; they are easy to write and easy to keep. The document becomes real at the first clause that costs the product manager, the sales organisation or the founder something they notice. An expert reads a working agreement by scanning for that clause first, and if there is none, concludes that the document was dictated and will not survive the quarter. At Indrayan the load-bearing clause is that no date is given to a customer without an engineering signature at a stated percentile, and it costs Deven Marfatia real deal velocity; that cost is the evidence the clause is genuine.

Estimates are corrupted by their audience, so experts ask who is listening

A number given to a peer over a desk and the same number given in a steering committee are different objects, because the second will be quoted and the first will not. The expert's habit is to ask, before answering, who will see this number and in what document. This is not evasiveness; it is a recognition that the conversion from estimate to commitment is the moment the information is destroyed, and that the conversion should be performed deliberately and by a named person rather than silently by whoever transcribes the meeting.

Decision rights are cheap to write and expensive to honour

The test of a decision clause is not whether it is written but whether the named decider has ever decided against someone more senior and had it stick. An expert asks for one logged instance from the previous quarter. Where none exists, the clause is aspirational, and the cheapest repair is to manufacture the instance deliberately on a low-stakes decision, publicly, so that the precedent exists before it is needed on a high-stakes one.

Many "how" decisions are product decisions in technical clothing

Latency budgets, offline behaviour, error taxonomy, retry semantics, and the shape of any interface that partners will build against for years are product decisions made inside technical documents. The expert reads the technical design document specifically hunting for them, and the tell is a sentence of the form "we will simply ..." attached to a user-visible behaviour. Conversely, every date a product manager sets is a technical decision, because it silently selects an architecture — the three-week version of a feature and the three-month version are rarely the same system, and the first is frequently not extensible into the second.

The swap rule is the only honest test of whether prioritisation exists

Ask a team what left the sprint the last time something urgent entered it. If nobody can name the displaced item, then nothing was displaced, and the work was absorbed by evenings, by quality, or by the item that will now be reported as late for unrelated reasons. The expert asks this question rather than asking whether the team has a prioritised backlog, because every team has a prioritised backlog and only some teams have prioritisation.

Set the interrupt budget at the observed rate, not the desired one

A budget of 10 per cent set against an observed injection of 22 per cent is violated in the first week and thereafter measures nothing. The expert sets it at 22, watches it for a quarter, and lowers it at the revision. The counter-intuitive consequence is that the first version of a good agreement usually legitimises the behaviour everyone wanted to stop — which is correct, because the budget's first job is to make the behaviour visible and its second job, a quarter later, is to reduce it.

Agreements decay at identifiable moments rather than continuously

They survive ordinary weeks and break at quarter end, at the first large customer escalation, at a re-organisation, at the arrival of a new vice-president, and after the first serious outage. The expert therefore schedules the revision immediately after those events rather than on a calendar cadence, and treats a calendar cadence as a fallback. The tell that an agreement has silently died is that it stops being cited in decisions; three weeks without a citation is a reliable signal.

Written agreements coordinate trust; they do not create it

Where trust exists, writing things down lets a distributed team, or a team with new joiners, or a team where somebody has less status than the others, coordinate on norms that would otherwise be invisible. Where trust is absent, the document becomes a weapon, cited to end arguments rather than to resolve them. The expert watches one behaviour to tell which world they are in: do engineers volunteer bad news before the deadline, unprompted? If they do, write the agreement. If they do not, the agreement is not the intervention.

The most common expert intervention is subtraction

Novice agreements are four to six pages and cover everything. Expert agreements are one page and cover the two or three things this team is currently failing at. Every clause carries a maintenance cost in attention, and a document with twenty clauses has none that anyone can recite from memory. A practical test: ask three members of the team to state one clause without looking. If they cannot, the document is too long regardless of how good the clauses are.

7How this varies — and where it does not

It is worth saying plainly that one part does not vary much. The decision-rights clause looks nearly identical across consumer, enterprise, platform and marketplace products, because the decisions that need assigning — ship a known bug, cut scope to hold a date, promise a date externally, declare an emergency — are structurally the same everywhere. Advice that suggests otherwise is usually selling a template.

The estimate and change clauses vary enormously, and the variation tracks a single question: how much of the incoming work is exogenous?

8Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Ekaaksh Money: converting a date question into a scope question

Aparna returns on Wednesday 15 July with three numbers rather than one. Full version one is 19.5 weeks at the eighty-fifth percentile — 27 November. By 16 October she can commit to 66 of the 96 items at the same confidence. And if the change protocol and the consultation clause are signed and held, she can commit to 85 of the 96.

She then does the thing that makes the arithmetic usable: she prices the signature. Eighty-five items instead of sixty-six is worth, on Ekaaksh's own merchant-acquisition model, roughly 1,900 additional merchants onboarded during the festive quarter, because the nineteen items include the bulk-mandate upload flow that mid-size merchants need. She is not asking Revathi Nambiar to sign a process document; she is asking her to sign for 1,900 merchants. That framing is why the clause gets signed, and it is the framing most product managers never construct because they have not decomposed the variance.

Indrayan Health Systems: when the date was signed before the estimate existed

Rohan's problem is harder because the commitment already exists. His options can be laid out with numbers. Liquidated damages run at 0.5 per cent of ₹6.2 crore per week, which is ₹3.1 lakh per week, capped at ₹31 lakh. Sneha's median is 7 December and her eighty-fifth percentile is 18 January, so the probability of missing 1 December is high — call it 80 per cent — and the expected lateness, conditional on being late, is about five weeks. Expected liquidated damages are therefore roughly 0.80 × 5 × ₹3.1 lakh ≈ ₹12.4 lakh.

That number understates the real exposure considerably, and recognising the understatement is the point. Indravati Hospitals Group has scheduled the annual maintenance contract on its legacy system to end on 31 December, at a saving of ₹46 lakh a year, and has committed to training 640 staff across six sites in November. A missed December go-live means either paying for a legacy renewal or running two systems, and it means re-training people who will by then have forgotten. The relationship cost is the cost that matters, and no contract clause prices it.

Rohan's alternative is a phased go-live negotiated directly with Indravati's chief operating officer: registration, billing and insurance pre-authorisation live at all six hospitals on 1 December — thirteen weeks of the twenty-one, achievable at the eighty-fifth percentile — with pharmacy, laboratory and ABDM linkage on 15 February. Commercially this requires an amendment to the milestone schedule so that 60 per cent of the licence value, ₹1.68 crore, is recognised at phase one. Indravati's finance head will want something for the amendment; the expected price is a 2 per cent discount, ₹12.4 lakh.

The arithmetic is, to within the precision of the inputs, a wash: a certain ₹12.4 lakh discount against an expected ₹12.4 lakh of liquidated damages. The numbers do not decide this. What decides it is that one path gives the hospital a working registration desk on the day it retires its old system and the other gives it a penalty cheque, and that the difference between those two outcomes is the next ₹6 crore. An expert does the arithmetic anyway, because the arithmetic is what makes the non-financial argument legible to a chief revenue officer who does not otherwise have to listen.

Induvadan Grid Systems: a good agreement that failed

Induvadan wrote a working agreement in January 2026 and it was, by the standards of this page, a good one: decision inventory, percentile-based dates, a swap rule, an interrupt budget. It was also six pages long, and it failed within two quarters.

The cause, when somebody finally classified the injections rather than counting them, was that about 70 per cent of unplanned work originated in field failures at a distribution company in eastern Maharashtra, and that those escalations arrived on the chief executive's phone and were forwarded to individual engineers by name. The chief executive had not signed the agreement and had not been asked to. Every clause in six pages was therefore irrelevant to seven-tenths of the problem.

The cost of catching it late was concrete. The firmware build required for a Bureau of Indian Standards re-certification submission missed its window by five weeks, which pushed Induvadan's participation in a discom tender worth roughly ₹22 crore over three years into the following cycle. The delay was attributed internally to "scope creep in the head-end system", which is the kind of explanation that guarantees the same outcome next year.

The recovery had three parts and one uncomfortable caveat. The six pages were cut to nine clauses. The interrupt budget spread across everyone was replaced by a named field-escalation rotation: one engineer fully allocated for a sprint, rather than 20 per cent of seven engineers, on the reasoning that interruption cost is convex — an engineer interrupted three times in a day loses considerably more than three times what an engineer interrupted once loses, a result consistent with Gloria Mark's research on resumption after interruption. And the chief executive signed exactly one clause: field escalations go to the rotation, never to an individual. The caveat is that a new vice-president of engineering arrived in June with political capital to spend, and spent some of it obtaining that signature. The document was necessary; it was not sufficient, and anyone who tells the Induvadan story as a triumph of process design has removed the part that did the work.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Estimate inflation deserves an additional word, because it is the failure mode organisations create deliberately and then fail to recognise. If a team is evaluated on estimate accuracy, it will produce accurate estimates within two quarters, and it will do so by inflating them until they are unfalsifiable. This is Goodhart's law operating exactly as described, and the defence is structural rather than exhortative: estimate accuracy must never appear in a performance conversation, and the agreement should say so in writing. The clause reads oddly to executives and is among the most valuable in the document.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Estimates versus probabilistic forecasting. The forecasting camp — Daniel Vacanti's Actionable Agile Metrics for Predictability (2015) is the clearest statement — rests on a real empirical observation: once items are sliced to comparable size, the count of items forecasts as well as the sum of estimates, and pointing consumes several engineer-hours per sprint to produce a number that adds nothing. The contract camp rests on an equally real observation: an enterprise customer needs a date for a scoped thing that has never been built, and throughput history over past work does not cover genuinely novel scope. What would have to be true for the forecasting camp to be wrong is that item sizes are not exchangeable — that the next 96 items are drawn from a different distribution than the last 52 — which is exactly the situation in a new domain, a new integration or a first hardware revision. What would have to be true for the contract camp to be wrong is that estimation effort produces no information beyond item count, which is well supported in steady-state product work and poorly supported at the frontier.

Contract versus operating model. Marty Cagan's position, stated most sharply in Empowered (2020), is that a carefully specified protocol for how features flow from product management to engineering entrenches the feature factory it was written to civilise. The steelman is strong: you can build a very high-functioning feature factory, and the artefact of a working agreement is evidence you have decided to. The counter-steelman is equally strong and less often stated: most teams in most companies genuinely are delivery teams with exogenous commitments — a regulator's deadline, a signed contract, a partner's release train — and telling them to be empowered without moving the profit-and-loss responsibility is advice they cannot act on. The agreement improves their Tuesday. What would settle it is evidence that teams with strong agreements plateau on outcome metrics while empowered teams keep improving; that evidence does not exist in any form either camp would accept.

Written versus relational. The case for writing rests on turnover, distribution across time zones, and equity: unwritten norms are invisible to new joiners and are enforced most heavily against people with the least status, so writing them down is a fairness intervention as much as a coordination one. The case against rests on a selection argument that is hard to dismiss — the teams that write agreements may simply be the teams that were already good at talking to each other, in which case the document is a marker and not a cause. Nobody has run the comparison that would separate these, and it is unlikely anyone will.

Interrupt budget versus dedicated rotation. The rotation camp argues from queueing and from the convexity of interruption cost: concentrating unplanned work on one person per sprint costs less total throughput than spreading 20 per cent across seven people, because the cost of an interruption is dominated by resumption rather than by the work itself. The budget camp argues that a rotation concentrates misery, erodes the domain knowledge of whoever is on it, and lets everyone else stop believing unplanned work exists. Induvadan's experience favours the rotation; a consumer team with small, frequent, low-context interruptions would favour the budget. The disagreement is genuinely unresolved and probably depends on the resumption cost of the particular work, which few teams measure.

Whether a product manager should ever produce a number. The case for is that a product manager who cannot sanity-check an estimate is a passive conduit, and that a straw estimate exposes a mismatch in mental models within minutes. The case against is anchoring, documented since Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 work and robust to expertise and to warnings: once the product manager's number is in the room, the team's number is contaminated and no one can tell by how much. The practical compromise most experts reach — the product manager may state a budget ("this is worth about three weeks to us") but never an estimate — is defensible and, it should be admitted, does not actually escape the anchoring objection.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways that are visible within a week. They negotiate the agreement before accepting the roadmap, because the agreement determines what the roadmap can mean. They ask for the spread before the estimate. They give away decisions publicly and early, on low-stakes items, so that the precedent exists before it is expensive. They pre-announce bad news — the item that crossed 1.5 times its estimate gets mentioned the same afternoon, not at the review — because the credibility that buys is the currency every later conversation spends. They keep a swap log and bring it to planning without being asked. Their document gets shorter each quarter rather than longer, and they can tell you which single clause is load-bearing this quarter and why it changed from last quarter's.

The deepest tell is how they talk about a missed date. The competent practitioner explains it: the integration was harder than expected, the partner's sandbox was down for four days. The expert decomposes it: of the eleven days of slippage, four were injected work, five were scope that arrived after commitment, and two were forecast noise — and then proposes a change to exactly one clause. The difference is not diligence. It is that the second person has a model in which the date is an output of a system with named inputs, and the first has a model in which the date is a prediction that turned out wrong.

12What each of them decides

Aparna Iyer does not give the 16 October date and does not refuse it either. On 15 July she offers leadership a choice with prices attached: the full version one at 27 November with eighty-five per cent confidence, or 85 of its 96 items by 16 October conditional on two signatures — the chief technology officer on the interrupt budget, and the head of compliance on a clause obliging her team to surface requirements at slice-commitment rather than at build time. She sets the interrupt budget at the observed 22 per cent rather than the aspirational 10, with a written plan to reach 14 by the October revision, and she accepts that this makes her look slower than the product manager in the next group who said yes to 16 October in ninety seconds. She will look correct in November, which is a long time to wait and is the actual cost of the practice.

Rohan Pillai goes to Indravati's chief operating officer rather than to his own chief revenue officer, which is the unusual move and the right one, because the customer has an interest in a working registration desk and Deven Marfatia has an interest in a signed contract, and those are different interests. He proposes the phased go-live, secures it at the cost of a 2 per cent discount, and then does the thing that will matter more: he adds one clause to Indrayan's working agreement stating that no go-live date appears in a contract without an engineering signature at the eighty-fifth percentile. The clause costs Deven deal velocity, Deven objects, and the chief executive signs it anyway — for now. Rohan understands that it will be tested at the next large deal, that the test will come at quarter end, and that the agreement's survival depends less on its drafting than on what happens in that one meeting.

Discussion questions.

1. Aparna's decomposition attributes 4.2 of 5.2 controllable weeks to the change and decision clauses, and 1.0 week to forecast noise. If the decomposition is right, why do organisations so reliably respond to a missed date by demanding better estimates? What would it take to change that response, and who would have to lose something?

2. Rohan's arithmetic came out a wash — ₹12.4 lakh of expected liquidated damages against a certain ₹12.4 lakh discount. When the numbers do not decide, what is the analysis for? Is a calculation that fails to discriminate between the options still worth performing, and to whom?

3. Induvadan's recovery required a chief executive's signature obtained by a newly arrived vice-president with political capital. If the mechanism was the signature rather than the document, what is the general lesson — that working agreements need executive sponsorship, or that the instrument is much weaker than its literature claims? What evidence would distinguish the two?

13Going deeper

How PMs alienate engineers. This is the failure catalogue the agreement exists to prevent; read it to work out which of your clauses are load-bearing and which are ornamental, because every clause worth writing corresponds to a specific listed failure.

Partnering with engineering and design leaders. The same negotiation conducted between functions rather than within a squad, where the counterparty has their own headcount, their own quality bar and their own performance narrative; it unlocks the ability to make an agreement stick above the team level.

Operating with a tech lead and architect. Everything the decision inventory assigns to engineering, and how a product manager stays genuinely useful inside those decisions rather than merely present at them.

The software development lifecycle. The stages the change protocol has to price differently — a change in design, in build, in hardening and in release are four different costs, and an agreement with one change price is wrong three times out of four.

Agile in practice. The operating context most agreements sit inside, and the source of the most common confusion on this topic: ceremonies are not agreements, and a team can run flawless ceremonies with no working agreement at all.

Kanban and flow. The alternative expression of the same discipline as work-in-progress limits and classes of service, which is the better instrument when intake is largely exogenous and the swap rule cannot bite.

The execution rhythm. The cadence at which the agreement's counters are actually read; an agreement without a standing slot where its three numbers are reviewed will decay on the schedule described in section six.

Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing. The mechanics of producing the number the estimate clause governs, including why the unit matters far less than the honesty of the spread attached to it.

Backlog management and refinement. Where scope growth is either caught or created, and therefore where the largest single term in the variance decomposition is actually controlled.

Ekaaksh Money, Indrayan Health Systems, Indravati Hospitals Group, Induvadan Grid Systems, Ekansh Retail Systems, Ekashila Bazaar and Ekagra Labs are fictional companies. Regulatory and market references — NPCI's UPI autopay framework, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, Bureau of Indian Standards certification and state distribution company tendering — are real context. All figures are illustrative and internally consistent; the statistical treatment assumes a normal approximation to the sum of weekly throughput, which is adequate at these sample sizes and understates tail risk.

Harike Labs: What a Date Means

Four months before a regulatory cut-off he cannot move, a product leader in Mohali must decide what his company's engineers and product managers actually owe each other — and discovers that the document meant to settle that question is the thing everyone is fighting about.

ISB Product Management Case Collection · Delivery & Technology · Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

1. Sunday Night, Mohali

At about nine on the evening of Sunday, 22 November 2026, Harjot Sekhon was sitting in the empty ground-floor conference room of Harike Labs in Mohali's IT City, waiting for a board pack he had not written and could not fully defend. The room smelled of the paint used on Friday to cover the marks left by a whiteboard that had hung there for three years, on which someone had drawn, in 2023, the diagram that became the company's Delivery Charter. Harjot, forty-one, vice-president of product, had been at Harike five years. Twice that week he had been told, by two people whose judgement he respected, that the charter was the only thing keeping the company from chaos, and that the charter was the reason it could no longer ship anything on a date.

Monday's board meeting had one substantive item: whether Harike Labs would confirm to its anchor customer, Kandi Finserv, and to its largest overseas account, Al Faridan Finance in Dubai, that the platform would meet the Reserve Bank of India's revised digital-lending disclosure requirements by 31 March 2027 and carry Al Faridan's multi-currency servicing changes at the same time. Devika Rao, the vice-president of engineering, had written to the board that she would sign no dated commitment beyond the regulatory work until the platform fork was merged. Ranjit Khurana, chief revenue officer, had already told the Dubai client, in writing, that both would land. Harjot's name was on the slide reconciling the two, and he had not been able to write it.

2. Harike Labs

Harike Labs was founded in 2017 by two engineers who had left a Noida banking-software firm and a former collections manager from a Ludhiana-based non-banking financial company. Their product, Tanda, was a loan-management and collections platform: it held the loan book after disbursal, generated repayment schedules, ran presentment against NPCI's e-mandate and UPI Autopay rails, managed restructuring and delinquency workflows, and produced the artefacts a lender's compliance team had to file. It was unglamorous software sold to unglamorous buyers — mid-sized NBFCs, two small finance banks, a co-lending platform — in a market where Lentra, Perfios, Yubi, Jocata and older core-banking vendors such as Nucleus Software and Intellect Design competed, and where the largest buyers, firms at the scale of Bajaj Finance or L&T Finance, tended to build their own.

By November 2026 Harike employed 212 people, 74 of them engineers, and carried annual recurring revenue of about ₹58 crore. Product and design sat in Mohali; the largest engineering groups were in Pune and Hyderabad; a platform group of nine, with the principal architect, worked from Bengaluru; Gulf customer success ran out of Dubai; and revenue was led from London, where two of the three growth markets — the UAE and UK specialist lending — were served.

One decision from the company's past shaped everything available to Harjot in November 2026. In March 2021, to win Kandi Finserv — then a ₹900 crore book, now above ₹4,000 crore — Harike had agreed to deploy Tanda as a dedicated single-tenant instance, hosted separately, with a master services agreement that named specific delivery dates for named capabilities and attached service credits to them. At the time the fork was two configuration files and a promise. By 2026 it was a materially different codebase, absorbing roughly 40 per cent of engineering capacity by any measure anyone trusted. The 2021 decision bought Harike the reference customer that made every later sale possible. It also wrote into a contract the idea that an engineering estimate could be a date.

The second inherited decision was the Delivery Charter itself. In early 2023, after a quarter in which Harike missed eleven customer commitments and lost four engineers, Devika Rao — then newly hired from a Pune product company — drafted a two-page working agreement. It said who decided what was built and why (product), who owned how and at what cost (engineering), that estimates were ranges with confidence levels and were never to become external dates without engineering's written assent, that scope inside a quarter could change only through a change-advisory board of three, and that engineering could decline work in writing. For six quarters, by nearly everyone's account, it worked.

3. The Industry

Indian lending technology in 2026 was shaped less by competitors than by the regulator's calendar. The Reserve Bank of India's digital-lending framework, tightened repeatedly since 2022, governed what a borrower had to be shown and when: the Key Fact Statement, the all-in annualised cost, cooling-off periods, the identity of the regulated entity behind any app. A revision published in mid-2026 changed the content and retention rules for those disclosures and set a compliance date of 31 March 2027. Separately, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's rules had begun to bite on consent artefacts and on how long collections recordings could be kept; NPCI had revised e-mandate presentment twice in eighteen months; and the Account Aggregator framework had become the default route for income verification.

For a vendor like Harike, this had two consequences. Regulatory work was neither optional nor negotiable in scope: a lender that could not produce a compliant disclosure on 1 April 2027 would stop lending, and would blame its software. And the compliance calendar was the industry's real roadmap, which meant every vendor's engineers spent a rising share of the year on work that generated no differentiation and no new revenue. Harike's own analysis put regulatory and rail-change work at 30 to 35 per cent of capacity across 2025 and 2026.

The overseas business complicated this. Al Faridan Finance, a Dubai consumer-finance house with a fast-growing salaried-borrower portfolio, had bought Tanda in 2024 precisely because Indian lending software was cheap, hardened by Indian regulatory churn and staffed in an overlapping time zone. But Al Faridan's requirements — multi-currency servicing, Arabic-first borrower communication, a profit-rate structure for its Islamic-finance line, a UAE data-residency posture — had almost nothing in common with the RBI work, and the UK prospects wanted something else again. Harike's sales narrative, that one platform served three regulatory geographies, was true in the deck and expensive in the codebase.

4. What Happened, and What Turned Out To Be Wrong

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. In January 2026 leadership approved a three-pillar plan: finish the RBI disclosure work by the end of the third fiscal quarter, merge the Kandi fork back into the multi-tenant platform by December 2026, and sign two Gulf logos. Faisal Rahman, the principal architect in Bengaluru, estimated the merge at "four to six months with four engineers," a figure that entered the board pack as "H1 FY27" and was never revisited in writing.

In April the RBI revision arrived with more scope than anyone had modelled — chiefly retention and reproducibility requirements that touched the archive layer. Nandita Iyer, head of regulatory affairs, flagged it within a week. Engineering re-estimated the disclosure work from eleven weeks to between eighteen and twenty-six. Under Clause 5 the range should have gone to customers as a range. What went out, in a newsletter drafted by marketing and approved in a hurry, was "ready well ahead of the deadline."

In June, Kandi Finserv's technology head invoked the 2021 agreement's service-credit clause over two missed dates, neither of which, on inspection, had been agreed by engineering in writing. Harike waived ₹41 lakh of fees to settle it. Finance recorded the waiver as a commercial concession and linked it, in no system, to the delivery record of the items in question.

In July, Ranjit Khurana closed Al Faridan's expansion — a second brand, a second currency, an October 2027 go-live — and in the closing email listed six capabilities against dates. Those dates came from a capacity model built in London out of Exhibit 2, engineering's own estimate-accuracy dashboard, which showed the team hitting its estimates better than nine times in ten. Ranjit said more than once, afterwards, that he had used engineering's numbers.

In September, the merge stalled. Aparna Nair, who managed the Kandi squad from Hyderabad, showed that the fork had diverged by some 380 files in areas the merge plan assumed were untouched, most added after March 2025 under mid-quarter changes approved individually and never assessed together. Faisal's four-to-six-month estimate, she argued, had been an estimate of a different piece of work. Faisal did not disagree, and pointed out that nobody had asked him to re-estimate.

In October, Devika instituted what engineering called a hard quarter: no new dated external commitments, no mid-quarter scope changes, every request routed through her. Attrition, which had run at 19 per cent annualised in the first half, fell. Two of the three change-board members stopped attending, because there was nothing to advise on. Product managers began negotiating directly with individual tech leads, which the charter had been written to prevent, and which nobody wrote down.

By November it had become clear that three things believed in January were wrong. The merge was not a four-to-six-month project; Aparna's revised range was nine to fourteen months, and Faisal's was still five to seven, and neither had been reconciled. The estimate-accuracy dashboard did not measure what the London capacity model had assumed it measured (see the footnote to Exhibit 2). And the charter, which everyone described as the company's protection, had been waived more often than it had been invoked (Exhibit 5).

5. The People

Harjot Sekhon — Vice-President, Product, Mohali
Owns the roadmap and, since 2024, the charter's stewardship. Position: the charter needs rewriting, not enforcing or scrapping. Incentive: his function's credibility rests on Harike shipping dates it names, and his six product managers are losing people to firms where the roadmap is not a negotiation. What he is not saying: he believes the 2021 single-tenant contract, not the charter, is the cause of everything, and that saying so at the board would sound like an attack on the founders.
Devika Rao — Vice-President, Engineering, Pune
Author of the charter; runs 74 engineers across three cities. Position: no new dated commitments until the fork is merged; the regulatory work will be delivered and nothing else will. Incentive: her retention numbers improved the moment she stopped accepting mid-quarter change, and she is measured on them. What she is not saying: she has told her three engineering managers that she would resign before signing the Al Faridan dates, and she has not audited how her own estimate-accuracy dashboard is calculated.
Ranjit Khurana — Chief Revenue Officer, London
Carries the Gulf, UK and India-enterprise number. Position: a software company that cannot name dates cannot sell to regulated lenders, and engineering's own dashboard says the dates are achievable. Incentive: his variable pay is weighted to new logo bookings, recognised at signature. What he is not saying: the six dates in his July email to Al Faridan were not reviewed by engineering, and one of the two Gulf "wins" in Exhibit 4 is a letter of intent with no committed value.
Aparna Nair — Engineering Manager, Kandi squad, Hyderabad
Twenty-two engineers on the single-tenant fork. Position: the merge cannot be scheduled until someone decides which of the fork's behaviours Kandi is contractually owed and which were favours. Incentive: her squad is the profit centre nobody thanks; if the merge succeeds, her team dissolves. What she is not saying: she has been quietly re-implementing three fork behaviours in the multi-tenant product without telling Devika, because she thinks it is the only way the merge ever starts.
Faisal Rahman — Principal Architect, Bengaluru
Owns the platform group and the merge design. Position: one quarter with no external commitments will save two years. Incentive: technical authority; the merge is the work he came to Harike to do. What he is not saying: his four-to-six-month estimate was made in a forty-minute conversation, was never written down with assumptions, and he now suspects it was wrong by a factor of two.
Nandita Iyer — Head of Regulatory Affairs, Mumbai
Interprets RBI, NPCI and DPDP obligations for the product. Position: 31 March 2027 is immovable and retention is the hard part. Incentive: she is the person in the room if a customer is found non-compliant. What she is not saying: outside counsel has given her a narrower reading of the retention clause worth roughly five weeks of engineering, and she has not circulated it, for fear it becomes the plan of record before the regulator's FAQ is published.
Lakshmi Menon — Director, Customer Success, Dubai
Owns Al Faridan and the Gulf accounts day to day. Position: the client will accept a later date if told now, and will not forgive being told in February. Incentive: renewal rates. What she is not saying: Al Faridan's chief operating officer has already asked her, informally, what Harike's engineering headcount on their account actually is, and she has not answered.
Sourav Dutta — Head of the Programme Office, Kolkata
Produces Exhibits 2, 3 and 5 and the board pack. Position: the company's problem is that nobody can say who committed what, to whom, when. Incentive: the existence of his function depends on the answer being process. What he is not saying: the commitment register he is about to put in front of the board was back-filled from email searches for the first quarter of 2026 and is not comparable across the year.

"I spent this quarter asking three tech leads for favours. When the charter was on, I could not change anything. When the hard quarter started, I could change anything as long as nobody wrote it down. I could not tell you which version was worse."

Re-ratify and enforce. This is the cleanest reading of Exhibit 6: the clauses were not the problem, the waivers were. It also asks Ranjit to retract a signed customer email while he carries the Series B narrative, and does nothing about the fact that under the charter's own procedure, in a hard quarter, the change board has stopped meeting.

Replace dates with a flow commitment. Abandon quarter-level date commitments for everything except the regulatory work. 9. The Deadline and the Constraints

The board met at ten on Monday. Harjot's slide had to say what Harike would commit to, to whom, and by when. The constraints were these. The 31 March 2027 date could not move; Nandita put the remaining work at eighteen to twenty-two weeks at the current allocation, which left no buffer, and the narrower reading of the retention clause that might save five weeks sat in an email she had not sent. Hiring was capped: the January plan allowed nine engineering hires in the second half, of which four had been made, and the Series B term sheet assumed headcount growth of no more than 15 per cent. The Kandi MSA carried service credits of up to ₹1.2 crore a year, of which ₹41 lakh was already waived. Al Faridan's expansion contract, worth ₹6.8 crore a year, had a termination-for-convenience clause with ninety days' notice, and the Dubai entity's financial year began in January. Two of the three change-board members had asked to be relieved. And the diligence checklist from the lead Series B investor, received on 14 November, carried a line Harjot had read several times: evidence of predictable delivery against externally communicated commitments, last four quarters.

10. The Night Before

At a quarter past eleven Sourav's board pack arrived. Exhibit 5 was in it, unchanged, with ₹28.6 crore in the at-risk column; Exhibit 2 was in it, on a slide titled Delivery Performance; the commitment register was in it with a footnote in six-point type. Devika had sent one line twenty minutes earlier: "Whatever you present, please do not present a date for Dubai." Ranjit had sent nothing since Friday, which in five years Harjot had learned to read as a position rather than an absence. Outside, the last Diwali lights were still up along the service road.

Harjot opened a blank document and typed a heading — What we will commit to — and then sat looking at it. The honest version of the slide, he thought, would begin by saying that nobody in the company currently knew what a date from Harike Labs meant. He was not sure whether that sentence was the most useful thing he could say to the board on Monday morning, or the last sentence he would say to them as vice-president of product.

11. Questions for Discussion

  1. What, precisely, is the working agreement between product and engineering at Harike Labs in November 2026? Distinguish the document from the practice, and identify where the two diverge.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same organisation in the same year and appear to contradict each other. Reconcile them. What, if anything, does Exhibit 2 legitimately measure, and what should the London capacity model have used instead?
  3. Exhibit 4 gives two incompatible answers about capacity, and Exhibit 5's "at risk" figure double-counts one customer's parent. How should a leadership team make a commitment decision when its own instrumentation is this weak — and what is the cost of waiting for better numbers?
  4. Devika's hard quarter improved attrition and suppressed recorded change, while informal change continued. Was it a success, a failure, or evidence that the charter was measuring the wrong thing? What would you have to observe to tell the difference?
  5. For each of the four options, trace the consequences through to June 2027 for Kandi Finserv, Al Faridan, the Series B diligence, and the engineers in Hyderabad. Which stakeholder bears the residual risk in each case, and does that person know it?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Harjot put on the slide, what does he say to the board about the March deadline and the Dubai dates, and what does he say to Devika, Ranjit and Aparna afterwards — in that order — to make whatever he has announced survive the week?
