The PM–Engineering Working Agreement

How decisions, estimates and changes flow between a product manager and the engineers who build the product — and why writing that down, on one page, is a variance-reduction device rather than a statement of good intentions.

1A Thursday evening in Bengaluru

At 8:20 on the evening of Thursday, 2 July 2026, Nandita Rao was still in the Indiranagar office of Ekatra Commerce Cloud, a company that sells order-management and returns software to about 340 direct-to-consumer brands in India. She had the sprint board on one screen and, on the other, an email she had sent eleven days earlier to Sudhir Menon, Ekatra's chief revenue officer, containing a sentence she was now trying to unwrite: "The invoicing compliance module will be live by end of July."

The module mattered. A wave of Ekatra's customers were about to cross into a lower turnover tier of the goods-and-services-tax e-invoicing mandate, which means that every business-to-business invoice they raise has to be registered with an Invoice Registration Portal and carry a government-issued reference number before it is legally valid. Ekatra's software raises those invoices. If the module is late, roughly ninety customers have to raise invoices by hand on the GST portal, at the exact moment their auditors are watching. Sudhir had already used Nandita's sentence in two renewal conversations worth, between them, about ₹2.4 crore of annual recurring revenue.

The engineers had not lied to her. Farhan Qureshi, who leads the Orders squad — six engineers in Bengaluru, one site-reliability engineer named Marek Zielinski in Warsaw — had given her a number: about thirty engineer-days of work. Nandita had done the division in her head, seen that thirty engineer-days across six engineers was "a bit over a week", added slack, and said end of July. Now, three weeks later, the squad had finished perhaps a third of it.

What had actually happened was visible on her second screen, if she cared to look. In the four sprints before this one, the squad had planned 201 engineer-days of work and been handed another 52 engineer-days of unplanned work after the sprint had started: a Razorpay webhook change, two customer escalations routed straight to Ritu Bhagat because she had once fixed something similar, a founder's request for a dashboard tile before a board meeting. Nobody had refused any of it. Nobody had recorded most of it either.

Nandita's instinct was to fix the estimate: to ask Farhan for "a real number this time", to add a buffer, to hold a longer planning meeting. That instinct is the one this page is about, and it is wrong. The estimate was not the broken part. What was broken was that Ekatra had no written answer to three questions: who decides what, what an estimate is allowed to become once it leaves the room, and what a mid-flight change costs. The instrument that answers those three questions is called a working agreement.

2What a working agreement is

A PM–engineering working agreement is a short, written, jointly authored document — one page is the right length — in which a specific product manager and a specific engineering team record four things: the decision rights (which decisions belong to whom, and what "decided" means), the estimate protocol (what an estimate is, who may produce one, and what may lawfully be done with the number afterwards), the change protocol (what counts as a change, how it enters the work, and what it displaces), and the escalation and revision clause (who breaks ties, and when the document gets rewritten). It is not a process framework, it is not a project plan, and it is not a set of values.

The problem it was invented to solve is old. In 1999, in Extreme Programming Explained, Kent Beck described what he called the planning game: a deliberate split in which "business" decides scope, priority and release dates, while "development" decides estimates, technical consequences and how work is sequenced within an iteration. Beck's insight was not that these two sets are different — everyone knew that — but that the fights happen where the sets touch, and that the touching points can be named in advance. The same period produced the definition of done in Scrum, formalised by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, which is really a working agreement about one word. The word "working agreement" itself came into common use through the retrospective tradition — Norm Kerth's Project Retrospectives (2001) and Esther Derby and Diana Larsen's Agile Retrospectives (2006) — where teams were taught to write down norms they kept breaking. Behind all of it sits older organisational-behaviour research: J. Richard Hackman's work on team launch, published as Leading Teams in 2002, found that teams which establish norms explicitly at the start outperform teams that let norms emerge, and Amy Edmondson's 1999 work on psychological safety explains why: a norm only exists if somebody is willing to say it out loud in front of the person it constrains.

The sentence Nandita could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "A working agreement is one page that says who decides what, what an estimate is allowed to become once it leaves this room, and what a change costs — and we rewrite it every quarter."

3How it actually works

The mechanics are unglamorous, which is why people skip them and write a poster instead. There are five steps, and the fourth and fifth are the ones practitioners leave implicit.

Step one: build a decision inventory. Sit with the team for forty minutes and list the decisions that actually occurred in the last month — not the decisions an org chart says exist. At Ekatra the list ran to nineteen items: whether a bug ships, the shape of the public webhook payload, whether to buy a GST-compliance vendor's API or build the integration, which customer escalation jumps the queue, what percentage of tenants get a rollout on day one, when the team pays down the queue-worker refactor. For each, name a decider, name who must be consulted, and classify it as reversible or not — the distinction Jeff Bezos popularised in his 1997 letter to shareholders as "type 2" and "type 1" doors. Reversible decisions go to whoever is closest to the work and are made fast; irreversible ones get the full consultation and a written rationale.

Step two: write the estimate protocol. Decide the unit (engineer-days, t-shirt sizes, story points — the unit matters far less than the discipline), state that estimates are produced by engineers and never by the PM, and — this is the clause that does the work — state what the PM is permitted to do with the number. A typical clause reads: "An estimate is a median, not a promise. External dates are quoted at the 80th percentile, computed as the median multiplied by the team's current spread factor, which is published every quarter." Add a re-estimate trigger: any item that passes 1.5× its estimate is re-estimated within a day, and the PM is told the same day.

Step three: write the change protocol. Define what counts as a change — new scope, altered acceptance criteria, a new constraint, or a re-prioritisation all count. Define one intake channel. Then the swap rule: nothing enters a sprint in flight unless something of comparable size leaves, and the PM, not an engineer, names what leaves. Then the interrupt budget: a stated share of capacity reserved for work nobody can foresee. Then the emergency override: who may pull the cord, and the requirement that every use is logged.

Step four, usually left implicit: price every clause. A clause that costs nobody anything changes nothing. If the team wants protection from mid-sprint injection, the price is that genuinely urgent things wait until the next morning's triage. If the PM wants a reliable date, the price is that she quotes a later one. Writing the price next to the clause converts a wish list into a trade, and it is the single strongest predictor of whether the agreement survives contact with a bad quarter.

Step five, also usually implicit: instrument it, and set a revision clock. Pick two or three counters — mid-sprint injection as a share of planned capacity, the spread factor, and median decision latency — and put them on the same page. Then name a date, ninety days out, when the agreement will be rewritten, and a standing rule that it is also rewritten after any production incident, any re-org, and any change of more than roughly a third of the team.

4The arithmetic, worked line by line

Nandita's promise of "end of July" was not careless arithmetic; it was arithmetic performed on the wrong quantity. Here is the calculation as the working agreement would require it to be done.

The Orders squad has six engineers. A two-week sprint contains ten working days, so nominal capacity is 60 engineer-days. Ceremonies, code review on other people's work, recruiting loops and the on-call baseline consume about 15 per cent, leaving 51 engineer-days of plannable capacity per sprint. That is the number Nandita had been dividing by.

It is the wrong number, because it assumes the sprint plan is what the squad works on. The four-sprint record says otherwise.

So effective capacity for planned work is 51 × (1 − 0.259) = 37.8 engineer-days per sprint, which matches the observed 36.3-day average almost exactly. Of that, the squad had agreed to give roughly 60 per cent to the compliance module, the rest going to two other commitments: 37.8 × 0.60 = 22.7 engineer-days per sprint.

Farhan's estimate was 30 engineer-days. At 22.7 per sprint, that is 30 ÷ 22.7 = 1.32 sprints, or 13.2 working days. Starting Monday 6 July, the median finish lands on Thursday 23 July.

But 30 was a median, and medians are wrong half the time. The agreement's estimate protocol requires the team's spread factor, computed from the last twelve completed items of comparable size: actual effort divided by estimated effort had a mean of 1.4 and an 80th percentile of 1.9. So the 80th-percentile effort is 30 × 1.9 = 57 engineer-days, which is 57 ÷ 22.7 = 2.51 sprints, or 25.1 working days: Friday 7 August.

Where does "end of July" sit? By Friday 31 July the squad will have spent 19 working days, or 19 × 2.27 = 43.1 engineer-days, on the module. That is 43.1 ÷ 30 = 1.44 times the estimate. Against a spread distribution with a mean of 1.4 and an 80th percentile of 1.9, a ratio of 1.44 is a little past the middle — call it a 55 per cent chance. Nandita had given her chief revenue officer a coin flip and called it a date.

The second pass: change one input

Now suppose the working agreement's change protocol actually bites, and mid-sprint injection falls from 25.9 per cent to 12 per cent — achieved not by refusing urgent work but by routing it through a single daily triage and honouring the swap rule. Two things move.

First, capacity: 51 × (1 − 0.12) = 44.9 engineer-days plannable, of which 60 per cent is 26.9 engineer-days per sprint for the module. Second, and less obviously, the spread narrows. A large part of the historical 1.9 was never estimation error at all — it was items sitting half-finished while their owner was pulled onto something else, then re-read and re-understood on return. With injection at 12 per cent, the squad's 80th-percentile ratio falls to about 1.5.

Median: 30 ÷ 26.9 = 1.12 sprints = 11.2 working days → Tuesday 21 July. Eightieth percentile: 30 × 1.5 = 45 engineer-days; 45 ÷ 26.9 = 1.67 sprints = 16.7 working days → Tuesday 28 July.

The promise Nandita had already made — end of July — goes from roughly a 55 per cent proposition to a comfortable one, and nobody worked a single hour faster. The whole of the improvement came from the change clause and none of it from better estimating. That is the argument of this page in one calculation: a working agreement is a device for reducing variance, not for improving accuracy, and the clause that reduces the most variance is almost never the one about estimates.

5Nuances a learner has to absorb

It is not agile mechanics, and confusing the two is the commonest error

A working agreement is silent on whether you run two-week sprints, Kanban with work-in-progress limits, or something you invented. It does not prescribe ceremonies. Teams that write down their meeting calendar, their story-point scale and their retrospective format have written a timetable, not an agreement. The test is simple: does the document say who decides, what a number means, and what a change costs? If not, it is process decoration. Teaching programmes that spend their engineering-collaboration module on agile mechanics reliably produce product managers who can run a stand-up and cannot hold a boundary.

Estimate, target, commitment and forecast are four different objects

Steve McConnell's Software Estimation (2006) makes the distinction crisply. An estimate is a statement about a probability distribution: our best analytical guess at effort. A target is a business desire: we want it by Diwali. A commitment is a promise made to someone outside the team. A forecast is an estimate combined with observed capacity and observed variance. Most organisational pain comes from a target walking into a room, being restated as an estimate, and walking out as a commitment. The estimate clause exists to make each conversion visible and to name who is allowed to perform it.

Decision rights are not a RACI chart

A RACI matrix maps roles onto activities and stops there. A working agreement adds the two things RACI never says: what happens when the people disagree, and what the default is if nobody decides in time. That second item — a decision service level, a stated window after which the decision defaults to the named decider acting alone — is what turns a chart into a mechanism. Ekatra's inventory gave every row a clock precisely because the previous quarter's slowest item had waited nine days for an answer nobody had been told they owned.

"PM owns the what, engineering owns the how" is a useful approximation that fails where it matters

The slogan is a reasonable first cut and a terrible final one. Every "how" that changes perceived latency, offline behaviour, error messages or the shape of an API that partners will build against for three years is a product decision wearing technical clothes. Every deadline is a technical decision, because it silently selects an architecture. The value of the agreement is precisely in the boundary cases the slogan cannot adjudicate, which is why the decision inventory has to be built from observed decisions rather than from the slogan.

A document cannot manufacture trust; it can only encode trust that exists

Edmondson's psychological-safety research is the relevant finding: norms only become real when somebody is willing to state them in front of the person they constrain. If engineers will not say "that date is fiction" out loud, they will not write it either, and the agreement will consist entirely of clauses that constrain engineering. That asymmetry is the fastest diagnostic available. Read any working agreement and ask: which clause costs the more powerful party something real? If there isn't one, the document was dictated, not agreed.

It governs flow, not correctness

A team can keep a perfect working agreement and build a product nobody wants. The agreement says nothing about whether the roadmap is right, whether the customer problem is real, or whether a decision was good — only about whether decisions get made, estimates get read honestly and changes get paid for. Process health and product outcomes are separate measurements and must never be substituted for each other in a review.

Agreements are per-team, and rolling them out as templates destroys the mechanism

The value lives in the forty minutes of argument in which a team discovers that two people held incompatible assumptions about who decides rollout percentages. Distributing a finished template across eleven squads preserves the artefact and throws away the mechanism. Templates are legitimate as prompts — "here are nineteen decisions other teams found they had to assign" — and illegitimate as standards.

They decay, and they decay at predictable moments

An agreement is kept until the first quarter-end crunch, the first large customer escalation, or the first new vice-president. It should therefore be re-read immediately after those events rather than on a calendar cadence, and it should be treated as void when more than roughly a third of the signatories have left the team. The revision clause is not administrative tidiness; it is what stops a stale document from becoming something people cite cynically.

6Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and small versus large

The decision-rights clause looks broadly the same everywhere. The other two vary a great deal, and the variation is driven by one question: where does the pressure on the team come from?

In a consumer product — Induj Payments, a Bengaluru consumer fintech running on the UPI rails, is a fair example — scope per change is small, iteration is fast and dates rarely bind. The estimate clause is nearly idle. What binds instead is experimentation: who may stop an experiment early, who reads the metric and declares a result, what the rollout gates are. A consumer working agreement is mostly about decision rights over experiments and releases.

In business-to-business software, dates are contractual. Ekatra's compliance module has a legal deadline; an enterprise customer schedules staff training around a go-live. The estimate clause becomes the load-bearing one, and the highest-value single line in the whole document is usually a sales-commitment rule: no date is given to a customer that an engineering lead has not signed at the 80th percentile. That clause costs the revenue organisation something real, which is why it is rare and why its presence tells you a great deal about a company.

In a marketplace — Ekavali Marketplace, which connects handloom clusters in Bhagalpur and Kanchipuram to urban buyers, is the shape to imagine — there are usually two product managers, one for supply and one for demand, sharing one engineering team. The scarce resource is not capacity but arbitration. The agreement's centre of gravity moves to how conflicting priorities are resolved, who holds the shared-platform budget, and what happens when neither side will yield. Marketplace teams that skip this clause do not have no priority order; they have one set by whoever escalates loudest, and it is invisible.

Stage changes things too. Below roughly fifteen engineers, the agreement should be very short and its most valuable clause is almost always the founder-override rule: founders are the largest single source of mid-sprint injection in every early-stage company, and naming the override — the founder may override anything, and every override is logged and reviewed on Friday — converts an untrackable force into a measurable one. In a large company the agreement must nest: a team-level agreement plus an interface agreement with the platform teams it depends on, and the escalation clause must map onto the actual management chain. An escalation path that names a person with no authority over either party is worse than none, because it consumes the one attempt the team had.

7Three common mistakes

The agreement as a wish list. The symptom, visible from outside, is a document full of values: we respect each other's time; we communicate openly; we assume good intent. The underlying misunderstanding is a belief that behaviour changes when intent is declared. The cheapest diagnostic is one question asked to the room: what did we agree to give up? If nobody can name a cost, nothing was agreed. A second, equally cheap test: read each clause and ask whether you could tell tomorrow morning whether it had been violated.

Quoting the median outside the room. The symptom is that every roadmap date is exactly the engineer's optimistic number and slips by thirty to fifty per cent with striking consistency. The misunderstanding is treating an estimate as a forecast — skipping both the capacity division and the spread multiplication that Nandita skipped. The diagnostic takes twenty minutes: pull the last six committed dates, compute actual effort divided by estimated effort for each, and look at the mean. If it is above about 1.3, the conversion rule is missing, and no amount of re-estimating will fix it.

The invisible interrupt. The symptom is a team completing around seventy per cent of its sprint plan, a retrospective that blames "estimation", and engineers working late without any of it showing up in a report. The misunderstanding is that capacity is being consumed by work that was never logged. The diagnostic is to ask the team, for two weeks only, to record every task they start that was not in the plan, with rough hours. The answer is almost always between twenty and thirty per cent, and seeing it written down does more than any exhortation.

Escalation by direct message. The symptom is that work appears which the PM first learns about in the sprint demo, usually traceable to a salesperson or a founder messaging an engineer directly. The misunderstanding is believing the intake channel exists because it is written down. The diagnostic is to ask three engineers to show their last five work items and say where each came from; if two or more arrived by private message, the channel is fictional and the clause needs a named consequence rather than a restatement.

8What good looks like

Handled well, Nandita's Thursday evening would have happened three weeks earlier and lasted ninety minutes. On 11 June, before saying anything to Sudhir, she sits with Farhan and the squad. They build the decision inventory. They look up the spread factor — 1.9 — and write it at the top of the page, not because it is flattering but because it is true. They compute the p50 and the p80 the way section four does, and they see the fifteen-day band.

Then Nandita does the thing that distinguishes the practice from the vocabulary: she takes the band to Sudhir and offers him a trade. She will commit externally to 7 August, which is later than he wants. In exchange she asks for two things: that the two renewal conversations quote 7 August, and that the customer-success team stop routing escalations to Ritu directly and send them to the daily triage instead. She also cuts scope — credit notes and the bulk-cancellation flow move to a second release in September — which pulls the p80 in by four days on its own.

Sudhir does not enjoy this conversation. He takes the deal because the alternative he is being offered is not "31 July" but "a 55 per cent chance of 31 July", and once the number is on the table he cannot un-know it. That is what the estimate clause is for: it does not make anyone braver, it makes the conversation impossible to hold in vague language.

9What Nandita decides

On Friday 3 July, Nandita writes one page. Four clauses, nineteen decision rows on the reverse, three counters at the bottom: injection rate, spread factor, median decision latency. She and Farhan sign it; so does their shared manager, the VP of product and engineering — without that third signature the agreement is a private treaty that the first executive escalation voids. She sets a revision date of 2 October.

Then she sends Sudhir a correction: the module's honest 80th-percentile date is 7 August, the median is 23 July, and Ekatra will tell customers 7 August. She sets the interrupt budget at 26 per cent — the observed rate, not the desired one — with a written plan to lower it to 15 per cent by the October revision. Setting it at the observed rate is the counter-intuitive move and the correct one: a budget set at an aspirational number is violated in week one and stops being a measurement of anything.

What to learn next follows directly. The failure modes this agreement prevents are catalogued under how PMs alienate engineers, and reading that list is the fastest way to understand which clauses are load-bearing in a given team. Beyond it lie two topics that assume the agreement exists: partnering with engineering and design leaders, which is the same negotiation conducted between functions rather than within a squad, and operating with a tech lead and architect, which is about the decisions the inventory assigns to engineering and how a PM stays useful inside them.

Two questions to sit with.

1. In the last working agreement you saw — written or unwritten — which clause cost the more powerful party something real? If you cannot find one, what does that tell you about how it was produced?

2. Nandita's injection rate was 26 per cent and her spread factor was 1.9. Suppose she could fix only one of the two, and fixing either takes a quarter. Which would you fix first, and what would you need to know about the source of the interruptions before answering?

Ekatra Commerce Cloud, Induj Payments and Ekavali Marketplace are fictional companies. Regulatory and market references — the GST e-invoicing mandate, the Invoice Registration Portal, UPI — are real context. Figures are illustrative and internally consistent.
